CausalChain: Reduced liver synthetic function (low albumin, high bilirubin) -> Alters nutritional and redox status in the hepatic microenvironment -> Modulates dendritic cell activation and T-cell priming -> Influences the efficacy and toxicity profile of immune checkpoint inhibitors in HCC
Hypothesis: The ALBI score not only reflects liver reserve but also directly modulates the hepatic immune microenvironment; specifically, optimal albumin–bilirubin balance (low ALBI grade) enhances antitumor immune responses and improves ICI efficacy while mitigating immune‐related hepatotoxicity in HCC patients.
Abstract: Recent clinical evidence has established the albumin‐bilirubin (ALBI) grade as a robust measure of liver functional reserve and a predictor of outcomes in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) across therapeutic modalities. Beyond its role as a surrogate for synthetic liver function, emerging observations suggest that the components of the ALBI grade, albumin and bilirubin, may exert immunomodulatory effects. Albumin not only reflects nutritional status but also influences systemic immune responses, while bilirubin possesses antioxidant and potentially anti‐inflammatory properties that could modulate antigen‐presenting and T-cell activity. We propose that the dynamic balance of albumin and bilirubin directly modulates the hepatic immune microenvironment. Specifically, patients with a low ALBI score (reflecting high albumin and low bilirubin) may exhibit a more active immune milieu that enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in HCC, whereas a high ALBI grade may predispose to both diminished antitumor immunity and increased vulnerability to immune‐related hepatotoxicity. This hypothesis has significant implications for patient selection and therapeutic stratification in immunotherapy trials for HCC.
